Where does preeclampsia occur in the body?

Abstract:
Although the mechanism of muscle wasting in end-stage renal disease is not fully understood, there is increasing evidence that acidosis induces muscle protein degradation and could therefore contribute to the loss of muscle protein stores of patients on hemodialysis, a prototypical state of chronic metabolic acidosis (CMA). Because body protein mass is controlled by the balance between synthesis and degradation, protein loss can occur as result of either increased breakdown, impaired synthesis, or both. Correction of acidosis may therefore help to maintain muscle mass and improve the health of patients with CMA. We evaluated whether alkalizing patients on hemodialysis might have a positive effect on protein synthesis and on nutritional parameters.

Eight chronic hemodialysis patients were treated daily with oral sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO(3)) supplementation for 10-14 days, yielding a pre-dialytic plasma bicarbonate concentration of 28.6 +/-1.6 mmol/l. The fractional synthesis rates (FSR) of muscle protein and albumin were obtained by the L-[(2)H(5)-ring]phenylalanine flooding technique.

Oral NaHCO(3 )supplementation induced a significant increase in serum bicarbonate (21.5 +/- 3.4 vs. 28.6 +/- 1.6 mmol/l; p = 0.018) and blood pH (7.41 vs. 7.46; p = 0.041). The FSR of muscle protein and the FSR of albumin did not change significantly (muscle protein: 2.1 +/- 0.2 vs. 2.0 +/- 0.5% per day, p = 0.39; albumin: 8.3 +/- 2.2 vs. 8.6 +/- 2.5% per day, p = 0.31). This is a retrospective study of twenty-two cases treated with TEVAR for TAI in our department from 2009 to 2014. Aortic injury was assessed in accordance with the recommendations of the Society of Vascular Surgery. We measured the aortic arch angle and the aortic arch index, based on the initial angio-CT scan, in each of the analyzed cases.

The mean aortic arch index and mean aortic arch angle were 6.8 cm and 58.3°, respectively, in the type I injury group; 4.4 cm and 45.9° in the type III group; 3.3 cm and 37° in the type IV group. There were substantial differences in both the aortic arch index and the aortic arch angle of the type III and IV groups. A multivariate analysis confirmed that the aortic arch angle was significantly associated with the occurrence of type III damage (OR 1.5; 95% CI 1.03-2.2).

Intravenous (IV) and inhalational (inh.) anesthetics are drugs that induce deep anesthesia during surgery. They act on the nervous system by modifying synaptic transmission. There are several differences between them which make one preferable to another depending on the situation:

### IV anesthesia

Ethrane (Somnoforme, Boehringer Ingelheim), methoxyflurane (Penthrane; Abbott), and thiopentone (Thesoral) are the most commonly used anesthetics for induction in intravenous anesthesia. The main advantage of IV anesthesia is its quickness of action, which provides early analgesia and a rapid recovery.

### Inhaled anesthesia

Isoflurane (Parecoxyl; Poulenc-Farmitalia), halothane (Fluothane; Abbott), enflurane (Ethrane, Boehringer Ingelheim), sevoflurane (Sufentanil; Abbott), and desflurane (Suprane, Baxter) are the most commonly used inhaled anesthetics. The main advantages of this method over IV anesthesia are its better control of depth of anesthesia and more rapid recovery.

Abstract:
To estimate changes in uterine myoma volume during pregnancy.

Review of departmental electronic perinatal database and medical records. Canadian Task Force Classification II-3.

Obstetrical ultrasound unit in an academic tertiary care center.

One hundred-seven patients diagnosed with uterine myomas during pregnancy and who had two or more obstetrical ultrasounds in different periods of pregnancy.

We analyzed the change in volume of uterine myomas between the first half of pregnancy (up until 19 weeks), third quarter (20-30 weeks), and last quarter (31 weeks to term). The volume of largest uterine myoma was calculated using the formula Volume (mm3)=Pi/6x(length mm)x(width mm)x(height mm).

The mean age of the population was 31+/-6 years. Between the first and the second study periods, the percentage of uterine myomas that decreased in size was 55.1% (95% CI: 43-66), with a mean decrease in volume of 35%+/-4%; while the percentage of uterine myomas that enlarged was 44.9% (95% CI: 34-56), with a mean increase in volume of 69%+/-11%. Between the second and the third study periods, 75% (95% CI: 56-87) became smaller, with a mean decrease in volume of 30%+/-3%; while 25% (95% CI: 13-43) enlarged, with a mean increase in volume of 102%+/-62%.

# Discussion
Bioinformatics is a relatively young discipline, born out of the need to organise, analyse and interpret the rapidly growing amount of biological data 1 . Today it represents an umbrella term which encompasses many different branches. In this paper we have focused on the interplay between Bioinformatics and Computer Science (BCS). BCS has emerged as a new cross-discipline that lies at the intersection between bioinformatics, information technology and computer science 2 . The study of BCS is still in its infancy and much remains to be understood about it. Its origins are rooted in the mid 1980s when computer scientists began to recognise new trends in biological data analysis that required sophisticated informatics tools 3 . In particular, the growth of molecular biology data, as well as the rise of high throughput technologies has led to an explosion in the amount of information available and a corresponding need for computational approaches to handle it. The emergence of BCS is therefore not surprising given that computer scientists are uniquely equipped to develop algorithms and tools with which to analyse, organise and visualise such data.
The first papers published under the umbrella term Bioinformatics in the late 1980s were computational analyses of biological sequences (e.g., DNA) 4 . Since then many other branches have emerged including comparative genomics, protein structure prediction, gene expression analysis and phylogenetics. As a consequence, bioinformatics has grown to include the entire life sciences field. The early publications were mainly theoretical in nature but with time they began to develop empirical studies which analysed large biological datasets 1 . This trend continued as computational techniques developed and biologists became more comfortable using such methods in their research.
As computer scientists became increasingly involved in the development of new bioinformatics tools, it was clear that a new discipline was emerging -the interdisciplinary study of informatics approaches to solving problems within the life sciences 1 . However, there was still debate as to whether this should be considered a sub-field or a distinct discipline with its own characteristics. As a result some scholars argued for the development of a separate computer science subfield dedicated to the use of computational techniques in biology (in contrast to the existing fields which were already well established such as theoretical computer science and artificial intelligence) 2 . This argument was further supported by the fact that bioinformatics, despite its interdisciplinary nature, has often been taught independently from other branches of computer science. Such a disconnect would inhibit researchers from being able to fully exploit the potential of information technology in their studies.
Bioinformatics is therefore an emerging discipline which has grown rapidly since its birth in the mid 1980s. As such, it is natural that there are many open questions about how best to teach it. Our survey of the literature on bioinformatics education has shown that while the field is growing, there is still no consensus on how best to teach the discipline. The most common approach seems to be an interdisciplinary one in which students learn both biological and computer science subjects simultaneously. There are however several problems with this. Firstly, it is not clear whether a combined approach would be appropriate since the disciplines of Bioinformatics and Computer Science are so disparate. Secondly, there is no guarantee that such an education would produce graduates who were able to apply their knowledge across different domains (as required by employers) 1 . Finally, it could result in students being dissatisfied with their degree programme if they found themselves having to study two unrelated fields without a clear link between them.
The alternative approach is to teach bioinformatics as a separate discipline within the computer science department. This would provide students with the opportunity to specialise in this field whilst still studying biological subjects and could also help to develop new algorithms which are tailored towards the needs of life scientists 1 . However, there are problems associated with such an approach since it is not clear whether bioinformatics should be considered a subfield of computer science or a new discipline in its own right.
In order for a discipline to become accepted as part of the curriculum at any university, it must first be recognised by academia 2 . In terms of education, this means that the discipline must be taught at undergraduate level and preferably also graduate level. If bioinformatics is to remain an interdisciplinary field then it must be taught within both biological and computer science departments in order for it to gain acceptance as a new subfield 1 . However, if Bioinformatics becomes its own discipline then this will require the establishment of new departments within universities which specialise exclusively in bioinformatics.
There are also concerns about whether bioinformatics should be taught as an interdisciplinary subject or as a separate discipline. The argument for teaching bioinformatics as a subfield of computer science is that it would provide students with the opportunity to learn about how computer science can be applied within life sciences 1 . It is likely that this approach would lead to students developing an in-depth knowledge of the theory behind such techniques which could then be applied to practical problems. However, the concern here is that by separating bioinformatics from other fields of computer science there may not be enough time left for students to learn about related topics such as data structures or machine learning 1 . In contrast, if bioinformatics were taught as a separate discipline then it would mean that students had more freedom in choosing their own specialisations. This could lead to a situation where graduates with different interests might find themselves unable to apply their knowledge across domains which is something employers often ask for (as evidenced by the fact that many job advertisements now require candidates to have knowledge of both biological and computer science subjects) 1 .
The study of bioinformatics has been growing exponentially in recent years. As a result, there is much debate about how best to teach it within universities around the world 2 . In this paper we have presented an overview of the field's history and discussed its current status. We have also surveyed the literature on bioinformatics education with the aim of identifying some key issues that should be addressed in order for the discipline to continue growing at such a rapid rate.
The first section provided a brief introduction into Bioinformatics which covered topics such as its history, definitions and applications. We then went on to present an overview of the current state of education in this field by looking at how it is taught around the world (in terms of both interdisciplinary versus separate approaches). Finally we discussed some issues associated with teaching bioinformatics including problems relating to its recognition as a discipline and whether or not graduates are able to apply their knowledge across domains.
We hope that this paper will provide readers with an overview of the current state of education in bioinformatics. It is intended to serve as a reference for academics who wish to learn more about the field and to help inform decisions about how best to teach it within universities around the world.

## Future directions
The field of bioinformatics has been growing rapidly over recent years but there are still many challenges which need to be addressed in order for this growth to continue. In particular, we would like to see more research into how best to teach bioinformatics within universities around the world. While it is clear that interdisciplinary approaches work well when teaching students about basic concepts (such as data structures or algorithms), there are concerns over whether such an approach would be suitable for developing graduates who are able to apply their knowledge across domains 1 .
We also believe that more research needs to be carried out into how best to teach bioinformatics in order to ensure that students have a good understanding of both biological and computer science subjects. In particular, we think it is important to develop modules which focus on specific areas such as machine learning or data structures since these topics often do not receive enough attention within standard curricula 1 .
Another area where more research needs to be done is how best to teach bioinformatics in the classroom. This includes questions about whether there are any advantages associated with teaching students about specific aspects of computer science (such as data structures or machine learning) compared to those who have not studied these topics 1 . We also believe that it would be useful for researchers to investigate how best to deliver teaching material within the context of a classroom setting since this may help make bioinformatics more accessible and relevant for students.
We hope that these suggestions will provide academics with some ideas about how they can improve education in the field of bioinformatics. By doing so, we believe that there is potential for the growth of this discipline to continue into the future. 14.

Question: Do cytokine concentrations in pancreatic juice predict the presence of pancreatic diseases?
Abstract:
Cytokine concentration in pancreatic juice of patients with pancreatic disease is unknown. Secretin stimulation allows endoscopic collection of pancreatic juice secreted into the duodenum. We aimed to evaluate the cytokine concentrations in pancreatic juice of patients with abdominal pain to discriminate presence from absence of pancreatic disease.

From January 2003-December 2004, consecutive patients with abdominal pain compatible with pancreatic origin were enrolled. Patients underwent upper endoscopy. Intravenous secretin (0.2 mug/kg) was given immediately before scope intubation. Pancreatic juice collected from the duodenum was immediately snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen until assays were performed. Pancreatic juice levels of interleukin-8, interleukin-6, intercellular adhesion molecule 1, and transforming growth factor-beta 1 were measured by modified enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. The final diagnosis was made by the primary gastroenterologist on the basis of medical history; laboratory, endoscopic, and imaging studies; and clinical follow-up. Fisher exact test and Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test were used for statistical analysis.

Of 130 patients screened, 118 met the inclusion criteria. Multivariate analysis revealed that only interleukin-8 was able to discriminate between normal pancreas and chronic pancreatitis (P = .011), pancreatic cancer (P = .044), and the presence of pancreatic diseases (P = .007). Individual cytokine concentrations were not significantly different in chronic pancreatitis compared with pancreatic cancer.

Randomized clinical trial with three parallel groups.

A hospital orthodontic department (Chesterfield Royal Hospital, UK).

Informed consent was obtained and participants were randomly allocated into one of three groups: (1) conventional pre-adjusted edgewise brackets and elastomeric ligatures; (2) conventional pre-adjusted edgewise brackets and Super Slick(®) low friction elastomeric ligatures; (3) Damon 3MX(®) passive self-ligating brackets. Space closure was undertaken on 0·019×0·025-inch stainless steel archwires with nickel-titanium coil springs. Participants were recalled at four weekly intervals. Abstract: A number of methods have been developed for using geographical information systems (GIS) data to map the spread and severity of infectious disease outbreaks, however these are not used widely in public health practice. We aimed to investigate barriers to use of GIS data in predicting outbreaks of infectious diseases among clinicians.
A 12-question online survey was conducted among UK-based NHS consultants working in infectious disease and public health using the Survey Monkey platform (http://www.surveymonkey.com/). The questions included: knowledge and use of GIS; access to, and quality of, data sources; potential barriers to the adoption of a predictive GIS model for outbreaks of infectious diseases in clinical practice.
30 NHS consultants responded (24 men and 6 women), 18 of whom had experience using or developing a GIS application, but only two who routinely used GIS as part of their day-to-day work. Only seven respondents reported access to high quality spatial data sets that would be useful for predicting outbreaks of infectious diseases. Respondents expressed willingness to use a predictive GIS model in clinical practice if it were: accurate and rapid; easy to use, free from charge; user-friendly with minimal training requirements; able to produce maps for the locality; and based on sound epidemiological evidence.
To be used widely by clinicians as part of routine surveillance for infectious disease outbreaks, GIS data need to be improved, and more accessible.

Abstract:
Depression is common in patients with diabetes and contributes to morbidity and mortality; however, its evaluation in this population is controversial. The objective of the present study was to assess the psychometric properties of a shortened version of the Center for Epidemiologic Studies-Depression Scale (CES-D) when used as a screening tool among persons with diabetes mellitus type II.

A multicenter, prospective, observational study was conducted to assess the psychometric properties of a shortened version of the CES-D scale when used as a screening instrument for depression in patients with diabetes. The sample consisted of 480 subjects who were randomly selected from five primary care clinics in New York City, New York. Patients completed self-administered questionnaires, including the shortened version of CES-D (21 items), the Montgomery–Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS), and demographic information.

Internal consistency was evaluated by assessing the Cronbach alpha coefficient and interitem correlations for each item in the scale, the corrected item total correlations, and principal component analyses were used to evaluate factor structure of the instrument. Receiver operating characteristic curve analysis was used to determine the optimum cutoff score that maximized sensitivity and specificity.

A shortened version of CES-D (21 items) with a 30 point cut off was found to have high internal consistency, good factor structure, and demonstrated the best balance between sensitivity and specificity for detecting clinically significant depressive symptoms among patients with diabetes mellitus type II.

Abstract:
To validate a clinical diagnostic tool, used by emergency physicians (EPs), to diagnose the central cause of patients presenting with vertigo, and to determine interrater reliability of this tool.

The first step focused on the presence of spontaneous nystagmus, the second on the direction of nystagmus, the third on head impulse test and the fourth on gait. The local standard practice, senior audiologist evaluation corroborated by neuroimaging when deemed appropriate, was considered the reference standard. Sensitivity and specificity of STANDING were calculated. On the first 30 patients, inter-observer agreement among EPs was also assessed.

Five EPs with limited experience in nystagmus assessment volunteered to participate in the present study enrolling 98 patients. Their average evaluation time was 9.9 ± 2.8 min (range 6-17). Central acute vertigo was suspected in 16 (16.3%) patients. There were 13 true positives, three false positives, 81 true negatives and one false negative, with a high sensitivity (92.9%, 95% CI 70-100%) and specificity (96.4%, 95% CI 93-38%) for central acute vertigo according to senior audiologist evaluation. The Cohen's kappas of the first, second, third and fourth steps of the STANDING were 0.86, 0.93, 0.73 and 0.78, respectively.
